extracted.intended_audience: authors, editors, copyeditors, and publishers using the University of Chicago editorial conventions
extracted.subtask_description: Copyediting and typesetting guidance following the University of Chicago Manual of Style: rules for italics, quotations, spelling, numerals, abbreviations, and punctuation as presented in the excerpt.

rubrics_metrics.name: Italicize foreign words and phrases
rubrics_metrics.description: Italicize words and phrases not in the English language; and single sentences or brief passages not of sufficient length to call for reduced type (see 75).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples given (e.g., 'the Darwinian Weltanschauung', 'Napoleon's coup d'état'); a long illustrative list of commonly italicized foreign words is provided (a priori, ennui, per annum, entrée, café, façade, naïve, résumé, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not italicize certain foreign usages
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not italicize foreign titles preceding names, or names of foreign institutions or places whose meaning or position in English would require roman type, and which either have no English equivalents or are preferred in the foreign form; nor words of everyday occurrence sufficiently anglicized though retaining accents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Père Lagrange, Freiherr von Schwenau; the German Reichstag, the Champs Elysées, the Museo delle Terme; and anglicized words like attaché, régime, naïve (listed with many others).

rubrics_metrics.name: Titles of publications in italics
rubrics_metrics.description: Titles of publications — books (including plays, essays, cycles of poems, and single poems of considerable length), pamphlets, treatises, tracts, documents, and periodicals — should be set in italics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Spencer, Principles of Sociology; A Midsummer Night's Dream; the Independent; the Chicago Tribune; Transactions of the Illinois Society for Child Study. Note: Some journals may have house practices (Botanical Gazette uses italics in text only).

rubrics_metrics.name: Books of the Bible and ancient manuscript titles in roman
rubrics_metrics.description: Books of the Bible, both canonical and apocryphal, and titles of ancient manuscripts, should be set in roman type.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See related rules (27 and 38) for context and exceptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not italicize certain bibliographical abbreviations
rubrics_metrics.description: In literary references, do not italicize abbreviations such as ibid., idem, loc. cit., op. cit., ad loc., s. v., supra, infra, passim, vide.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: By contrast, cf., i.e., e.g. should also not be italicized and are set with a thin space.

rubrics_metrics.name: Address line formatting
rubrics_metrics.description: Address lines in speeches, reports, etc., and primary address lines in letters should be set flush in a separate line, with nouns capitalized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'Mr. President, Ladies and Gentlemen:' and 'Mr. John Smith, 121 Dearborn Street, Chicago, Ill.' Set with capitalization per rule 43.

rubrics_metrics.name: Placement of titles/positions in signatures
rubrics_metrics.description: In signatures, the position or title added after the name: if one word, run into same line with the name; if more than one but no longer than the name, center the first letter under the name line and indent one em on the right; if longer than the name, center the name over the second line and set that flush.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'Arthur P. Maguire, Secretary' and multi-line examples like 'Carter H. Harrison / Mayor of Chicago'. Rules subject to exigencies of special cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of a), b), c) and letter suffixes
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a), b), c) etc. to indicate subdivisions (single parenthesis if beginning a paragraph, double parentheses if 'run in'); and use a, b, c, etc. affixed to verse, page, etc., to denote fractional parts (with hair-space where appropriate).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Luke 4:31a (with a hair-space).

rubrics_metrics.name: Letters to designate unknown quantities or labels
rubrics_metrics.description: Use letters to designate unknown quantities, lines, etc., in algebraic, geometrical, and similar matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples shown: ac + bc = (ia + b); the lines ad and AD; the wth power; and letters in legends referencing illustrations (e.g., 'At the point A above (see diagram)').

rubrics_metrics.name: Quotations set in roman and in quotation marks
rubrics_metrics.description: Put citations run into the text of a passage from an author in his own words between quotation marks and in roman type.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See rule 64 and related rules for various quotation contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quotations from different authors in sequence
rubrics_metrics.description: When quotations from different authors follow each other uninterrupted by intervening original matter, set each in quotation marks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See rule 65 for this situation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quotation of words with definitions or unusual terms
rubrics_metrics.description: Put a word or phrase accompanied by its definition, or an unusual/technical/ironical word or phrase, in quotation marks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'Drop-fold' means a page-number at the bottom of the page; 'slug'; quoted usages like 'lead' inserted between lines; 'so-called', 'self-styled'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Translations: give English equivalents in quotes
rubrics_metrics.description: In translations, give the English equivalent of a foreign word, phrase, or passage in quotation marks adjacent to the original.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Weltanschauung 'world-view'; Mommsen, Romische Geschichte ('History of Rome').

rubrics_metrics.name: Use quotes to direct attention to particular words or phrases
rubrics_metrics.description: Use quotation marks to indicate the particular word(s) to which attention is directed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: the term 'lynch law'; the phrase 'liberty of conscience'; the concepts 'good' and 'bad'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Serial titles and shorter work titles in quotation marks
rubrics_metrics.description: Serial titles and titles of shorter poems and subdivisions of works should be quoted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'English Men of Letters' series; Shelley's 'To a Skylark'; chapter or article titles like 'John Stuart Mill'. Note: some journals' house practices (Botanical Gazette) may differ in footnotes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Block (reduced) quotations criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Ordinarily, all prose extracts making three or more lines in the smaller type, and poetry citations of two lines or more, should be set in smaller type (block quotations). An isolated prose quotation that bears organic relation to the argument may be run into text.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A one- or two-line quotation closely preceded/followed by longer extracts set in smaller type may also be reduced for uniform appearance. See rule 75 for reduction guidance and rule 76 for point-size reduction specifics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reduced-type size conventions
rubrics_metrics.description: As a rule, reduce from 11-pt. and 10-pt. to 9-pt., from 9-pt. to 8-pt., from 8-pt. to 6-pt.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See rule 76 and 233 for details on reductions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reduced citations: omit quotation marks and italics
rubrics_metrics.description: Reduced citations should not have quotation marks, except as noted (e.g., multiple authors), nor should quotation marks, as a rule, be used in connection with italics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See rule 77; exceptions noted in rule 65.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quotation clarity: include ellipses and 'etc.' inside quotes when necessary
rubrics_metrics.description: Quotation marks should always include ellipses and the phrase 'etc.' when otherwise it would not be clear that they stand for omitted matter; perfect clearness in each case is the best criterion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrative examples show when 'etc.' belongs inside vs outside quotation marks depending on what it stands for (omitted matter of quotation vs something outside the quotation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Repeat opening quotation marks for multi-paragraph quotations
rubrics_metrics.description: Quoted prose matter broken into paragraphs should have the quotation marks repeated at the beginning of each paragraph.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See rule 79.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cleared quotation marks for alignment
rubrics_metrics.description: Where alignment is desired, quotation marks should be 'cleared' — i.e., should project beyond the line of alignment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example given illustrating left-projected opening quotes aligning with body text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of double and single quotation marks
rubrics_metrics.description: Double quotation marks are used for primary quotations; for a quotation within a quotation use single marks; alternate back to double for a third level, single for a fourth, and so on.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'The orator then proceeded: 'The dictionary tells us that "the words 'freedom' and 'liberty'..."'' '

rubrics_metrics.name: Spell out most civil and military titles and forms of address before names
rubrics_metrics.description: Spell out all civil and military titles, and forms of address, preceding the name, except Mr., Messrs., Mrs., Dr., Rev., Hon.; abbreviate Esquire (Esq.) following the name. Do not set Rev. or Hon. except in quotations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See rule 82 for details and parenthetical note on foreign equivalents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spell out given (Christian) names and 'von' as part of name
rubrics_metrics.description: Spell out Christian names (George, Charles, John — not Geo., Chas., Jno.) except where abbreviated in quoted matter or original signatures; also spell out 'von' as part of a person's name.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See rule 83 and accompanying alphabetization notes (a–e) for how to alphabetize hyphenated and particle-containing names.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alphabetization rules for surnames with particles or prefixes
rubrics_metrics.description: Hyphenated names are ordinarily alphabetized under the part after the hyphen; French/German particles 'de' and 'von' are listed under the following letter when written lower-case; Dutch 'Van' is regularly capitalized and listed under V; Spanish names with 'y' are listed under the name preceding 'y'; names beginning with 'Mc' are treated as if spelled 'Mac'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Henry Chandler-Taylor under Taylor; Emile de Rambeau under R; Van Maastricht under V; Gomez y Pineda under Gomez; 'Mc' names grouped with Mac.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spell out numbers under three digits (generally) in ordinary prose
rubrics_metrics.description: In ordinary reading matter, spell out all numbers of less than three digits unless of a statistical or technical character, or occurring in groups of six or more following each other in close succession.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat connected groups alike; do not mix figures and words within a group; if the largest contains three or more digits, use figures for all; 'per cent.' should use figures (e.g., '110 per cent.'). Examples illustrate when to spell versus use numerals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use round numbers as spelled words
rubrics_metrics.description: Round numbers (approximate figures in even units) are usually spelled out (e.g., 'five hundred' rather than '550' when approximate).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'a thesis of about three thousand words' but specific figures 'about 2,700' are given in numerals; '1,500' spelled 'fifteen hundred' if spelled out.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spell out numbers at beginning of sentences
rubrics_metrics.description: All numbers, no matter how high, commencing a sentence in ordinary reading matter should be spelled out; when impracticable, reconstruct the sentence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example rewrite suggested: 'The total number of those who went down with the ship was 593 men' instead of starting with '593 men...'. See rule 86.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sums of money spelling/figures rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Sums of money occurring in isolated cases in ordinary reading matter are spelled out; when several such numbers occur close together or in statistical character, use figures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'The admission was two dollars.' vs 'Admission: men, $2; women, $1; children, 25 cents.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Time of day: spelled out in ordinary prose, figures in statistical contexts
rubrics_metrics.description: Time of day in ordinary reading matter is written in words (at four; at half-past two in the afternoon; at seven o'clock); in statistical enumerations and always with A.M./P.M., use figures (at 4:15 P.M.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Omit 'o'clock' when using figures with A.M./P.M.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ages spelled out
rubrics_metrics.description: Write ages in words (eighty years and four months old; children between six and fourteen).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See rule 89.

rubrics_metrics.name: Numbers of centuries, sessions, military bodies spelled out
rubrics_metrics.description: Numbers of centuries, Egyptian dynasties, sessions of Congress, military bodies, political divisions, thoroughfares, etc., should be spelled out unless brevity is important.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: nineteenth century; Fifth Dynasty; Fifty-fourth Congress, Second Session; Fifth Avenue.

rubrics_metrics.name: References to decades in words
rubrics_metrics.description: Refer to particular decades in words (e.g., 'in the nineties').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See rule 91.

rubrics_metrics.name: Names of months spelled out (except in statistical contexts)
rubrics_metrics.description: Names of months are spelled out, except in statistical matter or long enumerations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'from January 1 to April 15' (omit st, d, th after dates).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use 'United States' spelled out in most contexts
rubrics_metrics.description: 'United States' should be spelled out except in quotations and such connections as military/political abbreviations (e.g., General Schofield, U. S. A.; U. S. S. 'Oregon'), and in footnotes/similar references (U. S. Geological Survey).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See rule 93 for contexts where abbreviations are acceptable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use full 'Railroad' and geographic words in names
rubrics_metrics.description: Use full forms such as 'Chicago, Milwaukee & St. Paul Railroad' (not R.R. or Ry.); use 'Fort' and 'Mount' in geographical appellations (Fort Wayne, Mount Elias).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See rule 94.

rubrics_metrics.name: Generally spell out names of publications
rubrics_metrics.description: In most cases, spell out all names of publications; modifications allowed for context, expediency, authoritative usage, and author's preference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If in doubt, spell out; good taste condones omission in this direction more readily than the opposite (see rule 95).

rubrics_metrics.name: Abbreviate state names in bibliographic/technical contexts
rubrics_metrics.description: Use standard abbreviations for names of U.S. states and territories following town names in bibliographies/technical matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A long list of standard two- to three-letter abbreviations is provided (e.g., Ala., Cal., Mass., N. Y., etc.). See rule 96.

rubrics_metrics.name: Firm-name abbreviations vary by context
rubrics_metrics.description: In technical matter (footnotes, bibliographies), abbreviate 'Company' and 'Brothers' and use '&' for 'and' in firm names; in nontechnical text, such words may be spelled out.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: The Macmillan Co., Macmillan & Co., Harper Bros.; vs 'Harper Brothers have recently published...'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use 'St.' before place names; omit for apostles/church fathers
rubrics_metrics.description: 'St.' is used before place names (St. Louis, St. Peter's Church) but preferably omitted when referring to apostles, evangelists, and church fathers (Luke, Paul, Augustine, not St. Luke, St. Paul, St. Augustine).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See rule 98.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard abbreviations for books of the Bible
rubrics_metrics.description: In references to Scripture passages, use standardized abbreviations for books of the Old and New Testaments and the Apocrypha (list provided).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Extensive list given: Gen., Ex., Lev., Num., Josh., I and II Sam., Matt., Mark, Luke, John, Acts, Rom., etc.; Apocrypha abbreviations also listed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bibliographical abbreviations for volume/number/chapter/page etc.
rubrics_metrics.description: In literary references, use abbreviations such as Vol. (Vols.), No. (Nos.), chap. (chaps.), Art., sec., p. (pp.), col. (cols.), vs. (vss.), l. (ll.), n. (nn.); use 'pp. 5-7' for inclusive pages, 'pp. 5, 6' for noncontiguous pages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When such phrases occur in isolated narrative text, it is often preferable to spell them out, especially at the beginning of a sentence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use metric unit abbreviations following numerals
rubrics_metrics.description: Use common metric symbols when following a numeral (1 m., 2 dm., 3 cm., 4 mm.; cm. = cubic meter, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: List of symbols given (c.c., c.mm., g. = gram; gr. = grain).

rubrics_metrics.name: Modern extracts: apply office style; older/essential cases follow original
rubrics_metrics.description: In extracts from modern authors whose spelling and punctuation differ but slightly from ours, use office style; in citations from Old English works or where a faithful rendering is essential, follow the original copy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Always quote titles accurately. See rule 102.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form possessives for names ending in s or sibilant
rubrics_metrics.description: Form possessive of proper names ending in s (if monosyllabic) by adding 's; if of more than one syllable, add an apostrophe alone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: King James's Version, Burns's poems, Marx's theories; Moses' law, Jesus' birth, Demosthenes' orations. Also 'for convenience' sake.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Use 'a' before sounded h and long w
rubrics_metrics.description: Before sounded h and long w, use 'a' as the indefinite article (a hotel, a harmonic, a historical, a union).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rule 104: choose 'a' for euphonious words that begin with sounded h or long w.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ligature use in Latin and other languages
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not use the ligature œ/æ in quotations from Latin or in anglicized derivatives from Latin/Greek where e has not been substituted; in quotations from Old English and some modern languages that employ it, use the ligature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Aeneid, Oedipus Tyrannus vs. Alfred, œuvres de Balzac, chef-d'oeuvre.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differentiate 'farther' and 'further'
rubrics_metrics.description: Use 'farther' to mean 'more remote' or spatial distance; use 'further' to mean 'moreover' or 'in addition'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: the farther end; further he suggested; a further reason.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preferred spellings list
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide authoritative preferred spellings for many commonly confused or variant forms (long list provided).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Extensive single-word spellings given (abridgment, archaeology, behavior, center, color, criticize, defense, honor, meter, neighbor, theater, traveler, etc.). See the full list in rule 107 and following pages.

rubrics_metrics.name: All punctuation printed in same type as preceding word
rubrics_metrics.description: All punctuation marks should be printed in the same type as the word or letter immediately preceding them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'With the cry of Banzai! the regiment stormed the hill;' punctuation matches preceding type (rule 108).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of period (full stop)
rubrics_metrics.description: A period is used to indicate the end of a complete sentence; put a period after all abbreviations except in mechanical exceptions or recognized technical symbols where periods are omitted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of abbreviations with periods: Macmillan & Co., Mr. Smith, St. Paul, no. i, Chas.; metric symbols treated as abbreviations (2 per cent., 10 mm.). Exceptions: chemical symbols (O, Fe), format of books (4to, 8vo), linguistic epoch abbreviations (IE, OE, MHG) and well-known journal initials (AJSL) often omit periods.

rubrics_metrics.name: No period after Roman numerals
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not use a period after Roman numerals even when they have ordinal value (Vol. IV; Louis XVI).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See rule 111.

rubrics_metrics.name: Omit period after running heads and certain headings
rubrics_metrics.description: Omit the period after running-heads, centered headlines, side-heads set in separate lines, cut-in heads, box-heads in tables, superscriptions and legends not forming complete sentences, date lines at top of communications, and after signatures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See rule 112 and cross-reference to rule 43 for signatures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Period placement with quotation marks and parentheses
rubrics_metrics.description: The period is placed inside quotation marks; place the period inside parentheses when the enclosed matter forms no part of the preceding sentence, otherwise place it outside.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rule 113: 'Tennyson's "In Memoriam."' Place period inside quotation marks without exception; parentheses rule illustrated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclamation point usage and placement
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the exclamation point to mark an outcry or an emphatic/ironical utterance; place it inside quotation marks when part of the quotation, otherwise outside.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'Long live the king!' 'The speaker went on: "This must not be!"' See rules 114–115.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interrogation point usage and placement
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the interrogation point to mark a query or express doubt; do not use it for indirect questions; place inside quotation marks only when it is part of the quotation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'Who is this?' vs indirect: He asked whether he was ill. See rules 116–117.

rubrics_metrics.name: Colon usage and placement rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a colon to mark a grammatical discontinuity greater than a semicolon and less than a period; commonly used to emphasize close connection between clauses, to separate a clause from an illustration/amplification, or to introduce a formal statement, extract, or speech; place colon outside quotation marks unless part of the quotation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a colon after salutatory phrases in letters and introductory remarks in speeches (My dear Mr. Brown:). Use a colon between chapter and verse in Scripture and between hours and minutes in times; colon often substitutes for 'namely' or 'as follows' when what follows are complete clauses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Semicolon usage
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a semicolon to mark a division of a sentence more independent than that marked by a comma; in enumerations use semicolons between lengthy or punctuated items; semicolon is placed inside quotation marks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include long enumerations with parenthetical comments and lists of officers (President; Vice-President; etc.). Rules 124–127 provide examples and contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comma usage principle
rubrics_metrics.description: The comma is used to indicate the smallest interruptions in continuity of thought or grammatical construction, the marking of which contributes to clearness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rule 128 introduces the comma and indicates its role in clarifying constructions; further specific comma rules follow beyond the excerpt.
